title: GAN-Based Brain MRI-to-CT Image Synthesis: A Comparative Review of Cross-Modality Translation Methods
content: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed  Tomography (CT) are complementary imaging modalities widely  used for the diagnosis and treatment planning of brain tumors.  While MRI provides superior soft-tissue contrast, CT supplies  essential electron density information required for applications  such as radiotherapy planning. However, acquiring both modal ities increases examination time, cost, and patient exposure to  ionizing radiation. Consequently, MRI-to-CT image synthesis has  emerged as a promising solution for generating synthetic CT  images directly from MRI scans using deep learning techniques.  This paper presents a comprehensive comparative review of  recent Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based approaches  for MRI-to-CT translation, with particular emphasis on Pix2Pix,  CycleGAN, and Attention-GAN architectures. The review ex amines their network designs, training strategies, preprocessing  pipelines, loss functions, and publicly available datasets. Fur thermore, their performance is analyzed using widely adopted  quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics, including Peak  Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Mea sure (SSIM), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Universal Quality  Index (UQI), Visual Information Fidelity (VIF), Normalized  Cross-Correlation (NCC), Hounsfield Unit (HU) analysis, and  expert perceptual assessment. The strengths, limitations, and  clinical applicability of each approach are critically discussed,  highlighting the trade-offs between paired and unpaired learning  frameworks and the benefits of attention mechanisms in preserv ing anatomical structures.  The review demonstrates that GAN-based MRI-to-CT trans lation has significant potential to reduce radiation exposure,  lower healthcare costs, and support MR-only clinical workflows.  Finally, current challenges and emerging research directions are  discussed to guide the development of more accurate, robust, and  clinically deployable cross-modality image synthesis models.
